[skia-sync] Merge upstream chrome/m151 bug fixes (#4489)

Context: companion mono/skia PR https://github.com/mono/skia/pull/286
Changes: https://github.com/mono/skia/compare/15fb073bf6...80ba1418a6

Same-milestone (m151 → m151) bug-fix sync that re-points the Skia submodule at
the merged mono/skia `skiasharp` tip (80ba1418a6), pulling in two upstream
Ganesh runtime fixes:

  * [Ganesh] Make sure stencil is cleared on kPreserve (b/534868067)
  * [Ganesh] If a resolve task fails to execute, unwind the dirty tracking
    (b/517973093)

This is deliberately not a version bump. Both upstream changes are internal
Ganesh implementation — nothing in include/, externals/skia/src/c/, or
externals/skia/include/c/ changed, and BUILD.gn/DEPS are untouched. As a result
regenerating the bindings produced no diff: the P/Invoke surface and every
generated binding are byte-for-byte identical, so there are no C# wrapper
changes.

Only the submodule pointer and cgmanifest.json's tracking fields move:

  * cgmanifest.json commitHash: 15fb073bf6… → 80ba1418a6…
  * cgmanifest.json upstream_merge_commit: 87424bcdba… → c3226a9bcd…
  * scripts/VERSIONS.txt, azure-templates-variables.yml, and
    sk_types.h SK_C_INCREMENT: unchanged (milestone stays 151, increment 0)

binding builds with 0 errors, and the full console test suite passes
(5711 passed, 0 failed, 182 skipped).

unresolvable on a read-only fs), so update-versions.ps1 / regenerate-bindings.ps1

4488.title: [WASM] Add preview-.NET WASM test job to catch exception-handling regressions
4488.author: mattleibow
4488.body:
[WASM] Add preview-.NET WASM test job to catch exception-handling regressions (#4488)

Context: https://github.com/mono/SkiaSharp/pull/4487

The emsdk 5.0.6 WASM libSkiaSharp can emit *legacy* wasm exception-handling
instructions, while .NET 11 links Blazor WASM apps with the *new* exnref model
(WASM_LEGACY_EXCEPTIONS=0). Mixing the two makes the app fail at runtime in the
browser, before a single line of user code runs:

    CompileError: WebAssembly.compileStreaming(): module uses a mix of legacy
    and new exception handling instructions

PR #4487 fixes the native build to emit new-EH instructions, but nothing in CI
would have caught the original regression. This adds that missing guard: it runs
the existing tests/SkiaSharp.Tests.Wasm suite under the preview .NET (net11) so an
EH mismatch — or any WASM breakage on the newer runtime — turns the build red.

The preview runtime is used for TESTS ONLY. net10 remains the default for every
other job, and the shipping TFMs are unchanged.

  * source/SkiaSharp.Build.props: add an opt-in UsePreviewTFM toggle (default
    off) that shifts the .NET version window forward one release (current=net11,
    previous=net10). Dropping the now-EOL net9.0 lets the test and the SkiaSharp
    binding it references build cleanly as net11.0 under a preview SDK, without
    tripping NETSDK1202 on the EOL net9.0-* platform TFMs.
  * scripts/infra/tests/tests-wasm.cake: add --previewtfm=true, which runs the
    same suite with -p:UsePreviewTFM=true. The cake is the run, not the infra.
  * scripts/azure-templates-jobs-bootstrapper.yml: add reusable installPreviewSdk
    and previewWorkloads parameters (install the preview SDK, pin global.json to
    it, install the requested workloads via the shared install-dotnet-workloads.ps1
    at the exact preview workload set) so other jobs can opt into a preview run.
  * scripts/azure-templates-variables.yml: add DOTNET_VERSION_PREVIEW and
    DOTNET_WORKLOAD_VERSION_PREVIEW (default DOTNET_VERSION stays net10).
  * scripts/azure-templates-stages-test.yml: add the tests_wasm_preview_linux job
    (consumes the native artifact; previewWorkloads=wasm-tools,android). android
    is required because the WASM restore still evaluates the -android TFMs of the
    referenced binding projects, exactly as the net10 job already does.

Both paths were validated locally against real 5.0.6/st,simd natives pulled from
CI artifacts: the new-EH lib runs the suite green (1180 total, 1081 passed, 0
failed, 99 skipped), and the legacy-EH lib fails with the CompileError above and
takes the job red via the runner's 300s timeout — a bounded failure, not a hang
or a silent pass.

Note: the preview .NET workload set, its manifests, and the emscripten 5.0.6 and
android packs are not on the dnceng public feeds by default (preview/late-leg
builds move to internal feeds), so the exact pinned versions were mirrored to
dotnet-public to make the pinned install reproducible in CI.

Co-authored-by: Matthew Leibowitz <mattleibow@live.com>
Co-authored-by: Copilot App <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

4370.title: [performance] Port SKColor -> SKColorF conversion to managed C#
4370.author: github-actions[bot]
4370.body:
Port SKColor -> SKColorF conversion to managed C# (#4370)

Fixes: https://github.com/mono/SkiaSharp/issues/4369

The implicit SKColor -> SKColorF conversion is pure per-channel math
(each 8-bit channel * 1/255, no gamma), yet every call crossed the
managed->native boundary via the sk_color4f_from_color P/Invoke - plus,
on the dynamic-load path, a cached-delegate indirection - and pinned an
output pointer. Because it is an implicit operator it is hit inside
per-item / per-frame loops: e.g. SKRuntimeEffect converts SKColor ->
SKColorF when setting a colour uniform, so an animated shader pays the
transition every frame.

Reimplement the operator in managed code as `channel * (1f/255f)` per
channel, marked AggressiveInlining. This removes the P/Invoke, the
delegate indirection and the pointer pin from a hot path. The operator
signature and public surface are unchanged, so there is no ABI break -
this is an internal implementation swap.

Faster (CI, BenchmarkDotNet 0.14, .NET 10), tracked via
ColorMathBenchmark.ToColorF (4096 colours through this operator),
PR build (managed) vs the previous released package (native):

  * Linux X64     12.7 us vs 20.6 us   ~1.6x   (0 B / 0 B)
  * Windows X64   13.6 us vs 25.6 us   ~1.9x   (0 B / 0 B)
  * macOS Arm64    5.1 us vs 12.9 us   ~2.5x   (0 B / 0 B)

Zero allocations before and after; the standalone SKColorFConvertBenchmark
(New vs Old) shows the same ~2x per-call win.

Behaviour-identical (bit-exact). SKColorFConvertEquivalenceTest compares
the managed operator against the native sk_color4f_from_color oracle by
reinterpreting the raw float bits (exact bits, not a tolerance) across all
256 grayscale values, each channel swept 0-255 with the others held
distinct (catches a swapped-channel port), and the 0/255 extremes, plus a
guard proving the comparison rejects both a swapped-R/B result and a naive
`x/255f`. The single-multiply-per-channel formula is bit-identical on every
runtime including x86 x87 (the 48-bit product fits the 64-bit extended
mantissa, so no double-rounding), verified on both the x64 (SSE) and x86
(x87) .NET Framework legs.

The reverse operator (SKColorF -> SKColor) is deliberately left native:
it is clamp -> *255 -> +0.5 -> floor, several dependent float ops that can
differ by 1 ULP under x87 extended precision, so a safe managed port would
need a native-math fallback and is a colder path - out of scope here.
ColorMathBenchmark.ToColor stays as a native sentinel so a future managed
regression would surface as a diverging ToColorF/ToColor ratio.

The equivalence test originally used BitConverter.SingleToInt32Bits, which
does not exist on .NET Framework, breaking the net48 test leg's compile;
it now uses an unsafe float->int32 reinterpret that is bit-identical on
every runtime.

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>
Co-authored-by: Matthew Leibowitz <mattleibow@live.com>

4385.title: Port single-value SKPMColor premultiply/unpremultiply to managed integer math
4385.author: github-actions[bot]
4385.body:
Port single-value SKPMColor premultiply/unpremultiply to managed integer math (#4385)

SKPMColor.PreMultiply(SKColor) and UnPreMultiply(SKPMColor) each round-tripped
a single colour through a native P/Invoke (sk_color_premultiply /
sk_color_unpremultiply) even though the underlying work is only a handful of
integer ops. Callers that convert one colour at a time — gradient ramps, palette
expansion, per-pixel software blends — hit these in tight loops, so the managed
to native transition cost dominated the actual conversion.

Reimplement both in managed C# using Skia's exact integer algorithms, so the
result is bit-exact with the native path for every input:

  * PreMultiply uses SkMulDiv255Round(c, a) = (p + (p >> 8)) >> 8, p = c*a + 128,
    per channel, with the opaque (a == 255) case passing through unchanged.
  * UnPreMultiply mirrors SkUnPreMultiply::gTable — a 256-entry
    round((255 << 24) / a) scale table built once at type init — then applies
    ApplyScale(scale, c) = (scale*c + (1 << 23)) >> 24, turning a per-call 32-bit
    divide into a table lookup.

The maths is integer-only, so it stays deterministic across all runtimes and
TFMs (no x87/float divergence, unlike float ports such as #4241) and matches the
native uint32 wrap even for out-of-gamut premultiplied colours where a channel
exceeds alpha. Only the method bodies change, so this is ABI-safe: the array
overloads stay native (already one P/Invoke per batch) and the cast operators are
untouched — both call these two methods, so they benefit automatically.

Correctness is proven, not assumed. SKPMColorEquivalenceTest exhaustively sweeps
alpha 0..255 x channel 0..255 for each R/G/B position against the native oracle
(sk_color_(un)premultiply) — a complete enumeration of every reachable input —
with distinct sentinels pinning the packing order, an opaque round-trip check,
and deliberately-wrong "teeth" guards proving the oracle comparison actually
detects divergence.

The Track - Benchmarks CI (ColorMathBenchmark) confirms the win with zero
allocations on every leg, managed vs the still-native nightly baseline on the
same runners:

  * Linux:   PreMultiply +32.9%, UnPreMultiply +31.6%
  * Windows: PreMultiply +24.1%, UnPreMultiply +20.9%
  * macOS:   PreMultiply +12.3%, UnPreMultiply  +2.4%

This also lays to rest the earlier "Linux regression" concern, which was
runner/baseline noise — Linux in fact benefits the most.

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>
Co-authored-by: Matthew Leibowitz <mattleibow@live.com>

4487.title: [WASM] Build emsdk 5.0.6 libs with new exnref exception handling
4487.author: mattleibow
4487.body:
[WASM] Build emsdk 5.0.6 libs with new exnref exception handling (#4487)

Context: https://github.com/mono/SkiaSharp/pull/4459

A .NET 11 Blazor WebAssembly app that references SkiaSharp links fine but
fails at runtime in a modern browser while instantiating the module:

    CompileError: WebAssembly.compileStreaming(): module uses a mix of
    legacy and new exception handling instructions (function #19801)

.NET 11 (preview 6+) links WASM apps with the *new* wasm exception-handling
model (exnref: WASM_LEGACY_EXCEPTIONS=0, emitting try_table/throw_ref).
#4459 correctly started shipping an emsdk 5.0.6 static library so net11.0+
apps link against a matching toolchain, but that library was still compiled
with only -fwasm-exceptions and no instruction-variant pin, so it emitted the
*legacy* wasm-EH instructions (try/catch). V8 refuses to compile a module that
mixes the two schemes, hence the CompileError. #4459 fixed the earlier link
failure; this fixes the remaining runtime EH mismatch.

Add a `_newexc` emscripten feature to native/wasm/build.cake that appends
`-s WASM_LEGACY_EXCEPTIONS=0` to both extra_cflags and extra_cflags_cc. This
is a codegen-affecting flag that must be passed at compile time (the .a build
produces wasm object files, so codegen happens during compile, not link), and
it has to cover both the C++ exceptions and the wasm setjmp/longjmp used by the
C dependencies (libjpeg-turbo, libpng, etc.). Enable the feature only on the
four 5.0.6 native matrix variants (st / mt / simd / simd+mt) in
scripts/azure-templates-stages-native-wasm.yml.

net8 (emsdk 3.1.34) and net9/net10 (emsdk 3.1.56) keep the legacy EH model to
match their runtimes, which predate the exnref proposal, so their build paths
are byte-identical (the flag is only added when `_newexc` is present). No
packaging or lib-selection changes are needed: `_`-prefixed feature tokens are
excluded from the artifact path, and the net11.0+ -> 5.0.6 selection already
exists from #4459.

Verified by rebuilding the 5.0.6 st and st,simd libraries from source: the
rebuilt .a disassembles to the new try_table/throw_ref instructions with no
legacy try-block/delegate/rethrow, and a net11.0 Blazor WASM app that failed
with the CompileError on the shipped (legacy-EH) lib now boots and renders with
SkiaSharp. net10 continues to link the legacy EH path (-lc++-except, no
-wasm-use-legacy-eh=0) and is unaffected.

Co-authored-by: Matthew Leibowitz <mattleibow@live.com>
Co-authored-by: Copilot App <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

4428.title: Restore SK_ENABLE_LEGACY_SHADERCONTEXT to fix CPU raster regression
4428.author: mattleibow
4428.body:
Restore SK_ENABLE_LEGACY_SHADERCONTEXT to fix CPU raster regression (#4428)

Fixes: https://github.com/mono/SkiaSharp/issues/4421
Context: https://skia.googlesource.com/skia/+/356c7267fa (Remove SK_DISABLE_LEGACY_SHADERCONTEXT)
Context: https://skia.googlesource.com/skia/+/1a15ed6b17 (Allow users to set SK_ENABLE_LEGACY_SHADERCONTEXT)
Related: #4463 (benchmark native cache-key fix), #4465 (LargeImageScaleBenchmark)

Starting with Skia milestone m146, software (CPU) rasterization of scaled or
tiled bitmaps regressed badly — high CPU, frame drops, and flicker that made
SKCanvasView nearly unusable on Windows. As diagnosed in #4421 by @janne-hmp,
upstream commit 356c7267fa dropped the default definition of
SK_ENABLE_LEGACY_SHADERCONTEXT from include/core/SkTypes.h. With the macro
undefined, SkShaderBase::makeContext() returns nullptr, so for kN32 + SrcOver
draws that carry a shader (a scaled/tiled bitmap builds a sampling shader)
SkBlitter::Choose can no longer use the hand-tuned SkARGB32_Shader_Blitter and
falls back to the generic raster-pipeline blitter for every draw.

The same upstream change (1a15ed6b17) deliberately made the macro user-settable
before removing its default, so defining it in the build is the sanctioned way
to restore the previous behaviour rather than a workaround.

Add -DSK_ENABLE_LEGACY_SHADERCONTEXT to extra_cflags, alongside the existing
SK_AVOID_SLOW_RASTER_PIPELINE_BLURS perf flag, in every CPU-raster libSkiaSharp
build (windows, macos, ios, tvos, linux, android, tizen, wasm; maccatalyst,
nanoserver and linuxnodeps inherit via delegation). This restores the exact
pre-m146 default across all platforms. winui (WinRT projection) and winui-angle
(ANGLE GL) are unaffected and left alone.

Verified two ways: @janne-hmp confirmed the PR artifacts resolve the regression
in their app, and a new regression benchmark (LargeImageScaleBenchmark, #4465 —
made measurable on CI by the native cache-key fix in #4463) shows the isolated
scaled-image path is 3x faster on macOS, ~5x on Windows, and up to ~18x on Linux
with the define restored. The raster-pipeline path is also notably load-sensitive
run-to-run, which matches the sustained-load throttling reported in #4421.

Note: SK_ENABLE_LEGACY_SHADERCONTEXT is legacy upstream and will eventually be
removed, so this restores prior behaviour rather than guaranteeing it long-term;
the underlying raster-pipeline image-sampling gap is being raised on skia-discuss.

Co-authored-by: Matthew Leibowitz <mattleibow@live.com>
Co-authored-by: Copilot App <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

4459.title: [WASM] Add Emscripten 5.0.6 static libraries for .NET 11
4459.author: ramezgerges
4459.body:
[WASM] Add Emscripten 5.0.6 static libraries for .NET 11 (#4459)

.NET 11 (preview 6+) links WASM apps with emsdk 5.0.6, replacing the 3.x
toolchain used by .NET 9/10. The buildTransitive targets selected the native
static library with an open-ended `net9.0+` -> Emscripten 3.1.56 rule, so a
net11.0 app was handed the 3.1.56 libSkiaSharp.a. A static library built with
Emscripten 3.x cannot be linked by emsdk 5.x (incompatible wasm object format),
producing a link failure.

Selection logic evaluated per TFM before the fix:

    | App TFM | emsdk the SDK links with | lib selected | result       |
    |---------|--------------------------|--------------|--------------|
    | net8.0  | 3.1.34                   | 3.1.34       | ok           |
    | net9.0  | 3.1.56                   | 3.1.56       | ok           |
    | net10.0 | 3.1.56                   | 3.1.56       | ok           |
    | net11.0 | 5.0.6                    | 3.1.56       | link failure |

Split the open-ended rule into bounded ranges and add a net11.0+ -> 5.0.6 entry,
wiring the new Emscripten version through the build and merge pipeline so the
packages actually ship it:

  * Consumer targets (shipped): SkiaSharp/HarfBuzzSharp NativeAssets.WebAssembly
    buildTransitive targets now route net9.0-net10.x -> 3.1.56, net11.0+ -> 5.0.6.
  * Repo-internal build/test: IncludeNativeAssets.{SkiaSharp,HarfBuzzSharp}.targets
    mirror the same split.
  * CI: add the four 5.0.6 variants (st/mt/simd/simd+mt) to the WASM build matrix
    and register the native_wasm_5_0_6_* artifacts in both native-merge lists.
  * Docs: update packages.md and updating-dotnet-version.md (remove the now-false
    ">=9.0 covers future versions" note; document the emsdk-per-SDK mapping).

Packaging globs (** / * over the version folder) pick up the new 5.0.6/
directory automatically, so no nuspec/csproj change is needed, and the WASM
Docker image already installs whatever EMSCRIPTEN_VERSION is passed.

The newest entry is intentionally left open-ended (net11.0+). net9.0 and net10.0
already share 3.1.56, and .NET 12+ may keep 5.0.6, so a future SDK that reuses
the same toolchain works with no code change. An entry is only capped with an
upper bound once a new SDK actually diverges (as net9.0-net10.x was capped at
< net11.0 when .NET 11 moved to 5.0.6). This convention is documented in
updating-dotnet-version.md.

Co-authored-by: Ramez Gerges <ramezragaa@proton.me>
Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

4438.title: Add a cross-platform perf tracker: benchmarks, sizes, unified dashboard
4438.author: mattleibow
4438.body:
Add a cross-platform perf-regression tracker: benchmarks, sizes, dashboard (#4438)

SkiaSharp had local benchmark tooling for one-off "old vs new" investigations
but no durable CI history. Once a performance PR merges, the old code is gone and
the new behaviour silently becomes the next baseline, so slow time/allocation
drift and native package-size growth were invisible across releases. This adds
continuous, persisted, cross-version tracking of benchmark time, allocations, and
NuGet/native artifact size, rendered as one interactive dashboard so regressions
surface instead of becoming the new normal. It is CI/tooling only — no existing
SkiaSharp library source is touched.

It also gives native regressions like #4421 a standing signal: the suite includes
a repro (BitmapDrawBenchmark, scaled vs unscaled DrawBitmap) whose ratio is a
hardware-independent indicator, so a platform hit by that shader-blitter fallback
stands out even before cross-OS normalization exists.

Version roles, split into released (on nuget.org) vs unreleased (CI/branch only):
  * nightly     -> newest -nightly.* on the EAP/CI feed (unreleased trend line)
  * latest      -> newest on nuget.org incl. preview/rc (released, still shipped)
  * curr/prev-stable, prev-major -> released stable baselines
  * pr          -> a source build of the branch (unreleased, ephemeral)
Benchmarks run Linux/Windows/macOS x the five roles; the pr source column runs
only on PR/dispatch (the nightly role already tracks main). The source build is
auto-gated on repo-deps.py's native cache-key: it only builds libSkiaSharp from
source when native inputs changed vs main, otherwise it downloads prebuilt
natives, keeping PR runs cheap.

Data model and persistence:
  * History lives on a dedicated aw-data git branch, not the Actions cache, so it
    survives for years. Each domain persists one merged summary the dashboard
    reads directly (benchmarks/index.json = {schema, legs}, sizes/index.json)
    plus additive plain-JSON raw captures under raw/<date>/... so summaries can be
    recomputed later. The ephemeral pr leg is dropped from persisted history.
  * The agent payload is uploaded on every run so any PR/dispatch run can download
    and preview exactly what would be persisted, but the actual commit to aw-data
    is gated in persist-aw-data.yml to successful same-repo runs whose head_branch
    is main. PR, branch, and fork runs never write to the branch; workflow_dispatch
    remains an admin override. Because this uses workflow_run (main's definition),
    persistence only begins after this PR merges and the first scheduled run lands.

Dashboard and tooling:
  * One ECharts page (scripts/infra/perf/templates/dashboard.html): metric tabs
    (Time/Allocations/Size), Absolute/Relative %/Log scales, searchable Group x
    Item multiselect, and a comparison table with PR / nightly / latest / stable
    columns. It ships as a self-contained per-run snapshot and also loads live
    from the aw-data raw URL, so the same file works locally, as an artifact, and
    against live history.
  * Shared tooling lives under scripts/infra/perf/ (_common.py for feed access and
    version-role resolution, merge_summaries.py, render_html.py, benchmarks/,
    sizes/, templates/). The size scripts moved here from .github/scripts/, and
    scripts/infra/perf/** is excluded in repo-deps.json since it is CI tooling with
    no effect on build caches (this also satisfies the public build's cache-config
    coverage validator).

Verified: both workflows green across all five roles on the three OSes plus the
source legs; the real agent payloads checked (benchmarks/index.json schema 2, 15
legs, no pr; sizes/index.json includes latest; raw is plain JSON); the
persist-aw-data copy/commit logic run against a real aw-data checkout adds
benchmarks/ and sizes/ additively without disturbing existing ai-triage data; and
the dashboard browser-verified rendering real data with distinct nightly and
latest columns.

3997.title: Fix native resource leak in SKImage.FromEncodedData(SKData, SKRectI)
3997.author: Copilot
3997.body:
Fix native resource leak in SKImage.FromEncodedData(SKData, SKRectI) (#3997)

The two-argument FromEncodedData(SKData, SKRectI) overload decoded an
intermediate full-size SKImage and then returned image.Subset(subset) via a
null-conditional one-liner:

    return FromEncodedData (data)?.Subset (subset);

When the requested subset is smaller than the full image, Subset() allocates a
new SkImage and returns a different wrapper, so the intermediate full-size image
was never disposed. Its native SkImage leaked until a GC eventually ran the
finalizer, which is exactly the case the same-instance disposal pattern used
elsewhere (ToRasterImage, other Subset call sites) exists to handle.

Apply that pattern: keep a reference to the intermediate, and dispose it only
when Subset() hands back a new instance.

    var image = FromEncodedData (data);
    if (image == null)
        return null;

    var result = image.Subset (subset);
    if (result != image)
        image.Dispose ();

    return result;

Output is unchanged; the only behavioral difference is that the intermediate is
now released deterministically instead of at finalization.

Add Pr3997ResourceLeakTest to lock this in:

  * FromEncodedDataWithSubsetDoesNotLeakIntermediateImage - the regression guard.
    It inspects the HandleDictionary registry and asserts only the returned
    subset stays registered after the call. Verified red on the old one-liner
    (Expected: 1, Actual: 2 - the leaked intermediate) and green on the fix. It
    runs in the serialized HandleDictionary threading collection so the
    alive-instance count is read in xUnit's non-parallel phase.
  * FromEncodedDataWithSubsetMatchesManualDecodeThenSubset and
    FromEncodedDataWithFullBoundsSubsetReturnsFullImage - parity guards proving
    the produced pixels are identical before and after the fix, for both the
    new-instance (partial subset) and same-instance (full bounds) branches.
  * FromEncodedDataWithSubsetThrowsForNullData - the null-argument contract.

The branch was also brought up to date with main (it was a milestone behind) and
the new test adapted to the repo's xunit.v3 migration ([Fact] rather than the
removed SkippableFact). Full CI is green: 0 test failures across all platforms.

4376.title: [performance] Make HarfBuzzSharp.Buffer.AddUtf8(string) allocation-free (pooled UTF-8 encode)
4376.author: github-actions[bot]
4376.body:
[performance] Make HarfBuzzSharp.Buffer.AddUtf8(string) allocation-free (#4376)

Fixes: https://github.com/mono/SkiaSharp/issues/4375

Buffer.AddUtf8(string) encoded the text with Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(utf8text),
which allocates a throwaway byte[] on every call, and then handed that array to
the native add. Its sibling AddUtf16(string) is already allocation-free, and
AddUtf8 sits on the canonical shaping hot path — SKShaper.Shape(string) ->
buffer.AddUtf8(text) -> SKCanvas.DrawShapedText — so the allocation is paid once
per shaped run / per frame for complex-script text.

Encode into a pooled ArrayPool<byte> buffer instead: rent GetMaxByteCount(len)
bytes, pin the string and the buffer, encode once with the unsafe
Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(char*, int, byte*, int) overload, pass the pointer and the
exact encoded byte count to the existing native AddUtf8(IntPtr, int, int, int),
and return the buffer in a finally. hb_buffer_add_utf8 consumes UTF-8 bytes and
copies them synchronously, and both old and new code use the framework's own
Encoding.UTF8, so the same bytes reach native and the shaping result is
bit-identical. Only the method body changes — the public signature is unchanged
(ABI-safe). The unsafe Encoding pointer overloads and ArrayPool<byte> exist on
all TFMs (net462 / netstandard2.0 included), so there is no #if split.

The rented buffer is intentionally oversized (GetMaxByteCount >= actual), so the
exact byteCount returned by GetBytes is passed to native, never utf8bytes.Length.

Edge behaviour is kept identical to the original Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes path,
now without its allocation or an extra branch:

  - null throws ArgumentNullException (explicit guard).
  - empty flows through the pooled path as a no-op: GetMaxByteCount(0) rents a
    small buffer, GetBytes writes 0 bytes, and AddUtf8(ptr, 0, ...) adds nothing
    — mirroring how AddUtf16(string) already handles the empty case.

Measured (BenchmarkDotNet, MemoryDiagnoser, in-process, net10.0, one reused
buffer reset with ClearContents between adds): zero managed bytes allocated on
every input (7-char word, ASCII sentence, 3-byte CJK, mixed paragraph) versus
32-120 B before, and never slower — the small time win comes from a single
GetMaxByteCount + GetBytes scan instead of encoding into a fresh array. The
0-allocation result is the durable claim; absolute ns vary by hardware/TFM.

Correctness is proven by an equivalence suite that compares AddUtf8(string)
against the verbatim original AddUtf8(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(text), 0, -1) path
on both the pre-shape buffer GlyphInfos and the post-shape glyphs / clusters /
advances (after GuessSegmentProperties + Font.Shape), across ASCII, whitespace,
2-byte, 3-byte CJK, decomposed combining marks, 4-byte emoji/surrogate pairs,
mixed scripts, and long strings that exercise larger pooled buffers; plus
explicit null-throws and empty-is-no-op cases grounded in main's behaviour, and
a teeth guard confirming the comparison detects a deliberately-wrong encode.

Co-authored-by: Matthew Leibowitz <mattleibow@live.com>
Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

4408.title: [performance] Remove per-call char[4] allocation in HarfBuzzSharp.Tag.Parse
4408.author: github-actions[bot]
4408.body:
[performance] Remove per-call char[4] allocation in HarfBuzzSharp.Tag.Parse (#4408)

Fixes: https://github.com/mono/SkiaSharp/issues/4407

HarfBuzzSharp.Tag.Parse(string) packed a tag by copying up to four chars into a
freshly allocated char[4] scratch buffer, space-padding the tail, then folding
the low byte of each slot into the uint. That scratch array is allocated on
every call, and tag parsing is hot during OpenType hydration — feature tags
("liga", "kern"), variation-axis tags ("wght", "wdth", "slnt"), and table tags
are often parsed in batches when configuring fonts and shaping features.

Rewrite Parse to read the first four chars directly and pad missing trailing
slots with spaces inline, with no scratch buffer. Packing semantics are
unchanged: null/empty -> Tag.None, short input space-padded, over-long input
truncated to four, and only the low byte of each UTF-16 code unit is kept.

Add an ABI-safe Parse(ReadOnlySpan<char>) overload and have the string overload
delegate to it via tag.AsSpan(), so callers can parse a slice of a larger string
without a substring allocation. The existing string signature is untouched.

This mirrors the already-merged SkiaSharp.SKFourByteTag.Parse optimization
(#4396); Tag is the HarfBuzzSharp sibling that still carried the old char[4]
path. Change is body + additive overload only, so it is ABI-safe.

Measured (BenchmarkDotNet, MemoryDiagnoser, net10.0) on a 22-tag batch: faster
and allocation-free, repeatable across runs. On .NET 10 both rows report zero
managed allocation because the JIT stack-allocates the non-escaping char[4], so
the win there is codegen (dropping the loops, bounds checks, and array
indexing); on net462 / netstandard2.0, which lack object stack allocation, the
old path additionally heap-allocated the char[4] per call, so those TFMs also
lose that allocation. No allocation regression on any TFM.

Correctness is pinned by precomputed [InlineData] constants (input + expected
packed uint) asserted against both the string and span overloads, plus a
verbatim copy of the original char[4] algorithm as a cross-check oracle, a
sliced-span case, null/empty -> None, a ToString round trip, and a teeth guard
proving the equivalence assertions discriminate a wrong value.

4388.title: [performance] Read SKShaper glyph results via zero-copy spans
4388.author: github-actions[bot]
4388.body:
[performance] Read SKShaper glyph results via zero-copy spans (#4388)

Fixes: https://github.com/mono/SkiaSharp/issues/4387

SKShaper.Shape(Buffer, float, float, SKFont) read the HarfBuzz shaping results
through buffer.GlyphInfos and buffer.GlyphPositions. Each of those getters
allocates a full array copy of the native glyph buffer — Buffer.GlyphInfos is
GetGlyphInfoSpan().ToArray() and Buffer.GlyphPositions is
GetGlyphPositionSpan().ToArray() — yet the extraction loop reads each element
exactly once. Both copies are pure per-shape waste, and this sits on the
canonical text hot path: SKCanvas.DrawShapedText -> SKShaper.Shape(string) ->
Shape(Buffer, ...), paid once per shaped run / per frame for complex-script or
shaped text.

Read the results through the existing zero-copy GetGlyphInfoSpan() /
GetGlyphPositionSpan() instead of the array getters:

    -var info = buffer.GlyphInfos;
    -var pos = buffer.GlyphPositions;
    +var info = buffer.GetGlyphInfoSpan();
    +var pos = buffer.GetGlyphPositionSpan();

The loop body is unchanged — indexing is identical on ReadOnlySpan<T>. The
buffer outlives the loop and both accessors call GC.KeepAlive(this), so the
spans over native memory stay valid; GlyphInfo / GlyphPosition are blittable,
so the produced Result is bit-identical to the array path. The three real
Result arrays (points / clusters / codepoints) are still built.

Managed C# only — private method body, no public SKShaper API change (ABI-safe),
no native / externals/skia change, rendering output unchanged.

~~ Proof ~~

Benchmark (SKShaperGlyphExtractionBenchmark, BenchmarkDotNet MemoryDiagnoser,
Linux x64 / net10.0, in-process toolchain) over a 3/24/96-glyph batch: ~33-44%
faster with 58-71% fewer bytes allocated per shape, e.g. 96 glyphs
772 ns / 7248 B -> 432 ns / 2112 B. Absolute ns are hardware/TFM-specific; the
ratios are the portable result.

Equivalence test (SKShaperGlyphExtractionTests, 8 cases): span-vs-array accessor
parity plus a ShapeResultMatchesArrayGetterOracle theory (Arabic
content-font.ttf + Latin segoeui.ttf at various offsets) asserting the shipped
Shape Result is bit-identical to an oracle recomputed from the array getters.
Non-vacuous: perturbing Shape (Codepoint + 1) turns the oracle cases red while
the empty-input and raw-parity cases stay green. 15/15 SKShaper tests pass
before and after.

Co-authored-by: Matthew Leibowitz <mattleibow@live.com>
Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>

4396.title: [performance] Remove per-call char[4] allocation in SKFourByteTag.Parse
4396.author: github-actions[bot]
4396.body:
[performance] Remove per-call char[4] allocation in SKFourByteTag.Parse (#4396)

SKFourByteTag.Parse(string) packed a tag by copying up to four chars into a
freshly allocated char[4] scratch buffer, space-padding the tail, then folding
the low byte of each slot into the uint. That scratch array is allocated on
every call, and tag parsing is hot during font/OpenType hydration — feature
tags ("liga", "kern"), variation-axis tags ("wght", "wdth", "slnt"), and table
tags are often parsed in batches when configuring a font.

Rewrite Parse to read the first four chars directly and pad missing trailing
slots with spaces inline, with no scratch buffer. Packing semantics are
unchanged: null/empty -> 0, short input space-padded, over-long input
truncated to four, and only the low byte of each UTF-16 code unit is kept.

Add an ABI-safe Parse(ReadOnlySpan<char>) overload and have the string
overload delegate to it via tag.AsSpan(), so callers can parse a slice of a
larger string without a substring allocation. The existing string signature is
untouched.

Measured on a 22-tag batch (Apple M3 Pro, .NET 10): 148 ns -> 26 ns, ~5.8x
faster. On modern .NET the JIT already stack-allocates the non-escaping char[4],
so the heap-allocation win is realized on runtimes without object stack
allocation (.NET Framework, Mono, WASM, AOT); everywhere the CPU-time win from
dropping the loops and bounds checks still applies.

~~ Tests ~~

The equivalence theory originally computed expected values at runtime from a
verbatim copy of the old char[4] algorithm, and one input used the range
operator ("...\"[..4]). On the .NET Framework test target the range operator
pulls in System.Index/System.Range, which are declared in both HarfBuzzSharp
and mscorlib, producing CS8356 and failing compilation of the whole Tests
(.NET Framework) job.

Replace the runtime oracle with precomputed [InlineData] constants (input +
expected packed uint), asserting both the string and span overloads against the
constant. This removes the range operator (fixing the .NET Framework build) and
makes the oracle immune to drifting alongside the code under test. Coverage
includes null/empty, padding, truncation, >0xFF low-byte truncation, and
surrogate code units.

~~ Review follow-up ~~

After the empty-span guard the length is always >= 1, so the length check on
the first character was dead; read tag[0] directly to drop the redundant branch
(behaviour unchanged, all parity tests still pass).

Companion: mono/skia#282

unspecified, so SubRunInitializer freed the backing memory before

the tuple with a struct that guarantees the allocator destructs before the
initializer frees the memory. This is the same fix already taken to
release/4.150.x in #4379; see mono/skia#282 for the full analysis.

commit; chrome_milestone (151) and upstream_merge_commit (0208108c7a) are
unchanged (same-milestone sync, no version bump). The upstream change is

impact -- binding regeneration produced zero diff and the full
SkiaSharp.Tests.Console suite passed (5614 passed, 0 failed, 182 skipped)

4345.title: Optimize SKColor hex parsing and add ReadOnlySpan<char> overloads
4345.author: mattleibow
4345.body:
[SkiaSharp] Optimize SKColor hex parsing and add ReadOnlySpan<char> overloads (#4345)

SKColor.Parse/TryParse sit on hot paths for code that hydrates colors from
XAML/CSS/JSON/theme files, but the old implementation parsed each channel with
byte.TryParse and the 6/8-digit forms with uint.TryParse (culture + NumberStyles
overhead), and carried a #if split where the net4x/netstandard2.0 path allocated
a `new string(char, 2)` per channel.

Replace that with a single allocation-free parser over ReadOnlySpan<char>
(Trim().TrimStart('#') + a length switch feeding small case-insensitive nibble
helpers), removing the #if split so one implementation serves every TFM. The
core now operates on a span, so re-basing to index 0 also lets the JIT drop the
per-access bounds checks in the fixed-length cases.

Add public span overloads so callers can parse a color out of a larger buffer
without allocating a substring:

    public static SKColor Parse (ReadOnlySpan<char> hexString);
    public static bool TryParse (ReadOnlySpan<char> hexString, out SKColor color);

The existing string overloads delegate to these via AsSpan(), matching the
pattern already used in SKFont, SKTextBlob, and friends. These are pure
additions, so the change is ABI-safe.

Behavior is preserved for every input the old code accepted, with one
intentional tightening: whitespace directly after '#' in the 6/8-digit forms
(e.g. "# 12345") was previously accepted as a side effect of
NumberStyles.HexNumber's AllowLeadingWhite and is now rejected, matching the
stricter behavior the 3/4-digit path already had. Parsing stays
case-insensitive.

This is a pure-managed change with no interop: SKColor is a readonly struct
wrapping a single uint, and neither the parse methods nor the private
TryParseNibble/TryParseByte helpers call into native Skia (no SkiaApi/sk_*,
DllImport/LibraryImport, Marshal, or stackalloc/fixed). No C API or generated
bindings are touched, so no native rebuild is required.

Measured on net10.0 (Apple M3 Pro, BenchmarkDotNet), zero allocations and
~1.4-2.3x faster across all shapes: "#FFF" 8.4ns -> 3.8ns, "#FFFF" 9.4ns ->
4.0ns, "#FFFFFF" 7.0ns -> 4.8ns, "#FFFFFFFF" 8.9ns -> 6.0ns, and invalid
fast-reject 3.7ns -> 1.7ns.

Adds SKColorTest coverage (whitespace, case-insensitivity, null/empty,
named-color rejection, span overloads, slice parsing) plus benchmark projects
documenting the strategy shootout, the span-vs-string comparison, and the
public New-vs-Old numbers.

native source fixes had to be carried: all five M150 backports the fork was
holding are now upstream in m151. Only two integration touch-ups were needed.

~~ C API include path ~~

m151 flattened include/private/base/* into include/private/* and removed the
private/base/ subdirectory. The one affected C API file was fixed in the fork
(SkTemplates.h include path), with no C function added, removed, or changed.

~~ Native build config (partition_alloc) ~~

m151 introduced src/partition_alloc/, whose BUILD.gn by default imports
${skia_partition_alloc_dir}/partition_alloc.gni. Our DEPS does not vendor
partition_alloc, so skia_use_partition_alloc=false is added to the gn args in
every clang platform's native/**/build.cake to opt into the bundled
src/partition_alloc/noop/ fallback. The default is is_clang (true on every
platform we ship), so the override is required. linux and wasm set it on both
the libSkiaSharp and libHarfBuzzSharp GnNinja calls; macos/ios/tvos/windows/
tizen/android set it on libSkiaSharp only (HarfBuzzSharp there builds via
xcodebuild/msbuild/ndk-build/tizen, not gn). Per known-gotchas.md #23 the arg
lives in build.cake, not --gnArgs.

~~ Submodule pin ~~

Re-pins externals/skia to 5209f4a49b55, the merge commit of fork PR #274 on the
stable skiasharp branch (tree-identical to the integration tip 68e1c7fe3c90),
and sets the cgmanifest Skia repo reference to match.

~~ Release-notes support tiers ~~

Updates the hand-maintained support block in scripts/infra/docs/versions.json
to stable [4.148, 4.150] / preview [4.151]: 4.148 stays Chrome Extended-stable
for a few more days, 4.150 (our RC line) goes stable imminently, and 4.151
becomes the in-flight preview. Drop 4.148 once Google retires extended-stable.

Full CI is green: build 158573 succeeded across all native platforms
(Windows/macOS/Linux/WASM/Tizen/Android/iOS/tvOS), managed build, API diff,
tests, and samples.
